item.title: The Self Is a Gift and a Burden
item.description:
Authenticity

The Self Is a Gift and a Burden

The thing that makes us human is also what often makes us unhappy.

Posted July 20, 2026

Key points
  • We spend our lives preoccupied with the self, yet some of our happiest moments are during hypo-egoic states.
  • There is no one single, true self inside each of us.
  • Self-esteem can be seen as an internal gauge of how valued and accepted we feel.
  • People who are more satisfied with themselves generally have a higher quality of life.

In the 1960s, psychologist Gordon Gallup conducted a series of now-classic animal experiments. Gallup marked the foreheads of anesthetized chimpanzees with a red dye. Upon waking, the chimps looked in a mirror, and just as many humans would have done, touched the red spot on their foreheads. This recognition of their own reflection became evidence that the chimps possessed rudimentary self-awareness.

Source: Vilkasss/Pixabay

Self-awareness is just one piece of the kaleidoscopic construct at the center of our lives – the self. Nearly everything we do is through it or in the service of it. An entire industry tells us how to protect, improve, and elevate it.

Yet, the story of the self involves a paradox. All our devout preoccupation with it is also what fuels our unhappiness. In fact, some of our most gratifying moments – in leisure, work, relationships, spirituality – occur during hypo-egoic states, when we temporarily forget our self-improvement ambitions.

Social psychologist Mark Leary has studied the self for 50 years. He defines it as “the cognitive apparatus that underlies conscious self-awareness” – akin to a negotiator mediating the different facets of our thoughts, emotions, motives and behavior. Among Leary’s biggest insights is that self-awareness – a far more complex version of what Gallup demonstrated with chimps – is what sets us most apart from other animals. Our capacity to think about ourselves in abstract ways, Leary argues, is what led humans to create a world dramatically different than the one we evolved in. It’s what has given us all our individual and collective accomplishments. But it has come at a cost. People don’t always recognize how nearly non-stop their self-related thoughts are, Leary points out, and how many are unnecessary or even work against their own interests. Learning how to handle all that self-reflective thinking more effectively, he suggests, could improve the quality of our lives.

Here’s Dr. Leary, in his own words, on five common myths and beliefs about the self.

There is a single, authentic true self inside each of us.

False. We are multifaceted – there is no single, absolutely true thing that a person is. We have different parts and pieces, and we change from situation to situation. We don’t want people to be hypocritical or dishonest – I think that’s what we’re arguing against when we say, “Be authentic.” But I also think authenticity is often over-glorified. If someone does something horrible and justifies it as being authentic, that’s not so good.

We should strive to raise our self-esteem, because high self-esteem is key to success in life.

False. While it’s true that high self-esteem is related to many good outcomes, it isn’t always their cause. It’s often a correlate. We shouldn’t try to raise self-esteem artificially: if someone is truly awful, do we really want them thinking, “I am a great person, and I feel wonderful about myself”? Self-esteem is an internal gauge of how valued and accepted we feel. The analogy I use is a car’s fuel gauge. Your car stops, and the fuel gauge reads empty. Would we say, “The car won’t run until we fix that E problem.” No, E is just the gauge. The car stopped because it had no fuel. When you feel accepted and valued, it feels good, so you keep behaving in those ways. Self-esteem isn’t creating the positive outcomes – your behavior is, by earning you social support. Even academic motivations are often social ones. Why should an “A” on my assignment make me feel good unless it brings positive consequences down the road that people value? The things that raise self-esteem are the things that make us feel more accepted (at least within our peer group). Self-esteem is a self-evaluation, but it’s related to other people’s reactions.

Knowing yourself deeply is the path to fulfillment and wisdom.

Neither true nor false. Knowing yourself – understanding your strengths, weaknesses and how you cope with life – helps you navigate the world better. You’ll likely make better decisions when you are well-informed, as opposed to carrying misconceptions about yourself. But it won’t necessarily create a wonderful or fulfilling life, because so many other factors are involved. Also, it’s hard to be honest about ourselves, particularly about our weaknesses and liabilities.

Being happy with who you are is a foundation of the good life.

Mostly true. Certainly, people who are more satisfied with themselves have a higher quality of life. However, the cause-and-effect direction is unclear: Do I have a higher quality of life because I feel good about myself, or do I feel good because my quality of life is high? If you were really unhappy with every aspect of yourself, I don’t think you’d have a high quality of life. I think it’s beneficial to strive for a life where you are generally pleased with your situation and characteristics – even if not 100 percent. When I was young, I used to wonder how much bad I should accept before I was unhappy with a day. I came back from school, thinking “I had a terrible day!” but upon reflection, I’d realize that not every minute had been awful. There were bad parts and good parts. As long as at least 85 percent of the day was okay, I decided it was a good day. We can apply the same principle to how we evaluate ourselves. None of us is satisfied with 100 percent of ourselves, but we all can find some things to be happy with.

Relentless self-improvement paradoxically makes people suffer more, since it is incompatible with being content.

I’ll go with the middle-of-the-road answer. If you are always trying to improve in every situation, you won’t be very content because you are always focused on deficiency. Indeed, some of our best moments are when the self goes quiet. The Stoic philosophers stressed ongoing improvement, but cautioned against becoming obsessive about it, because it can backfire. There is a happy medium. I want to be better tomorrow than I am today – but if I worry about it incessantly, I’ll never reach a point where I’m happy or at peace with myself.

Many thanks to Mark Leary for his time and insights. Dr. Leary is Garonzik Distinguished Professor Emeritus of Psychology and Neuroscience at Duke University.

item.title: Dealing With Grief as We Age
item.description:
Grief

Dealing With Grief as We Age

Coping with grief is highly individualized, but there are tips to help all of us.

Posted July 20, 2026

Key points
  • We all grieve differently.
  • By the time we reach our senior years, we've experienced many types of loss.
  • Author Kate Doerge believes we can choose how we grieve.
Source: Ali Ahmad Danesh/Pexels

By the time we reach our senior years, we have experienced a wide range of grief. When we talk about loss and grief, we’re not only talking about the loss of loved ones, but also other situations, such as declining health and the loss of physical ability, cognitive function, occupational identity, and our role in society.

Often, we’ve experienced multiple layers of loss at once, such as losing loved ones, dealing with health changes, losing the ability to do what we once could, and experiencing a shift in family and community roles.

Even if the loss occurred a long time ago, we can still be easily triggered by certain events, such as anniversaries, birthdays, or everyday reminders that send us down the rabbit hole of sadness and grief. This is especially common after losing a loved one. It is very common for grief to resurface years later. It’s all a normal part of love and memory.

How We Grieve and How Grief Shows Up

Grief is a natural response to loss. It should never be considered a weakness. Everyone grieves in their own way. There’s no timetable or “correct” method for healing.

Grief can show up psychologically, such as through sadness, anger, guilt, or confusion, and physically, such as fatigue, trouble sleeping, changes in appetite, or aches and tension. It’s important to care for the body. Grief often comes in waves.

Some people cry easily; others feel more numb or keep busy to avoid feeling the loss. Others want to talk, while still others prefer quiet reflection. Some, especially poets, grieve by writing poetry. Writing can help us meet every moment.

When we’re grieving, the feeling does not always go away; it simply changes in intensity. It takes time. It takes support.

Nurturing the Light

“Nurturing the light” doesn’t mean ignoring the pain associated with grief; it means making a small, steady space for comfort, meaning, and connection.

Remember that grief and light can coexist: Even in sorrow, there are threads of meaning, connection, and resilience. This means fostering gratitude, sharing cherished memories, engaging in creative expression, meditation, prayer, or being in the company of kindred spirits who understand what you’re feeling.

After grief has settled, there’s often an opportunity to gain more clarity about life. People often develop a deeper understanding of what truly matters.

Questions to Ask

Here are some questions to ask yourself or a loved one who is grieving:

  • What’s most important to you?
  • What is no longer important?
  • What do you want to share?
  • What are the small and big ways you can reach for joy?
  • How do you want to shine your light? What impact do you want to make?

Choosing How to Grieve

In her book Reimagining Grief, Kate Doerge asserts that we choose how we move through grief. She lost her 16-year-old daughter, Penny, to neurofibromatosis, a condition diagnosed when Penny was a little girl. She described her daughter as someone who was a ray of light. Although Penny became quite ill at the end of her life, Doerge decided to celebrate her during her final days, surrounded by light and happiness with so many people who loved her.

“You don’t have a choice in which cards come up, but you can and will decide how you play them. How you play them will determine your happiness in life,” she says. In fact, how you play them will determine everything in life.

She referenced her father’s comment on her wedding day: “I just want you to know it isn’t always going to be like this. You’re just at the beginning of your life, and I know it feels like everything is going to always be perfect and beautiful, but the reality is that life will challenge you in ways you can’t even imagine.”

She learned that it was up to her to decide how to respond to life’s challenges.

Doerge offered these five action steps for moving through the grieving process:

  1. Connect with others.
  2. Celebrate the beloveds.
  3. Be open to the signs.
  4. Get moving.
  5. Turn pain into purpose.

The Five Stages of Grief

In contrast, psychiatrist Elisabeth Kübler-Ross’s list of the five stages of grief was formulated to help us know what to expect. The stages provide a useful framework, but they do not necessarily offer guidance for navigating the day-to-day challenges of grief.

  • Denial (shock and disbelief)
  • Anger (resentment and frustration)
  • Bargaining (seeking a way out)
  • Depression (sadness and withdrawal)
  • Acceptance (finding a way forward)

Summary

In the end, we have to find a way to accept a new way of being in light of our loss, whether it is the loss of a loved one or a profound change in our own health, identity, or abilities. There is no single roadmap through grief. Different writers and clinicians have offered different ways of understanding the journey. Kate Doerge emphasizes the choices we make in responding to loss, while Elisabeth Kübler-Ross offered a framework for understanding the emotional landscape of grief. Together, these perspectives remind us that while grief is universal, how we move through it is deeply personal.

item.title: Activating the Subconscious to Promote Healing
item.description:
Unconscious

Activating the Subconscious to Promote Healing

Belief in rituals, sacred spaces, placebos, or therapy helps improve health.

Posted July 20, 2026

Key points
  • If we believe an intervention is going to help us, it often does.
  • Prayer, healing rites, and rituals can appeal to the subconscious to help with health.
  • The relationship between the subconscious and well-being is a very underappreciated association in medicine.
Source: Skreidzeleu/Shutterstock

As the driver of your attention, the subconscious helps create your narrative and your reality. This means that when you participate in and believe in healing rites for any kind of well-being, you encourage your subconscious to help achieve the desired result.

Medical journals, history, and literature are full of examples, the most prominent being that of the placebo. Study after study tells us that if we believe a treatment is going to help us—even if it’s actually a sugar pill—it often does (Price et al., 2008; Kaptchuk & Miller, 2018).

For as long as there have been civilizations, we’ve had healing rites and rituals that appeal to the subconscious for help. If we become quiet in prayer, for example, we don’t just seek help and guidance from a higher power; we also become calm, slow our breathing, think of the outcomes we want, and engage the subconscious to help us on our way.

If we pray in a more spirited way, we can feel joy and euphoria. Similarly, sometimes we go to great lengths to visit sacred spaces to find healing environments. It’s why people around the world make treks to pray and bathe at the Catholic shrine in Lourdes, to meditate and practice qigong at the Buddhist Shaolin Temple in China, to pray at the Western Wall in Jerusalem, or to balance their energy at the New Age vortex sites in Arizona.

In the Gospel of Matthew, there is a story about Jesus healing a paralyzed man. Before his physical recovery, the man receives the Lord’s forgiveness. On its surface, the miracle of the story appears to be his regaining the ability to walk. But what if the power in this interaction arose from having his sins forgiven? What if being freed of the burden of his inner torment allowed the man to overcome a psychological burden?

In the Torah book of Leviticus, physical maladies such as leprosy were often understood as signs of spiritual disorder, much as subconscious distress can aggravate physical illness. That is why priests were charged with carrying out rituals meant to support healing.

I believe it’s likely that even our most ancient and revered stories of healing involved the subconscious in the process. I’ve seen similar scenarios happen in my own medical practice.

For instance, I have been asked to consult on cases of adolescents who were hospitalized for a mysterious inability to walk. After ruling out a medical cause, I worked with the patients’ subconscious to help them move past their trauma or fear, which allowed them to regain their ability to use their legs (Anbar, 2008).

My experiences in these cases and similar ones demonstrate that remarkable healings can be achieved through work with the subconscious.

Takeaway

The relationship between the subconscious and well-being is one of the most underappreciated associations in medicine. Whether through prayer, ritual, community, or the therapeutic encounter, the meaning we attach to healing experiences shapes how our bodies respond. This isn't mysticism, but rather it's neuroscience. Acknowledging these pathways expands what medicine can offer.
